title: Phrases
objectives: Student can read a two-to-five-word phrase as one continuous sound, with no gap between words.
Student can carry a word's final vowel across the join into the next word, and drop a waṣl hamzah in flight.
Student can hold a phrase-length rhythm — shaddas held and madds counted — without the length collapsing as the phrase gets longer.

slides.heading: The phrase you have said more often than any other
body: Read the basmalah. Now read it again, the way you have been reading words in 2-10: carefully, one word at a time.
The result is unmistakable, and you will hear it yourself: bismi. Allāhi. ar-raḥmāni. ar-raḥīmi.
Four separate words, three glottal stops that should not be there, and a phrase that no longer sounds like the phrase.
Careful word-reading and correct phrase-reading are two different skills — and the first one, done too well, breaks the second.
Today you learn to let go of the word.

audio.cue: 1:1 — bismi-llāhi-r-raḥmāni-r-raḥīm. Three waṣl hamzahs, all silent. One unbroken sound.

slides.heading: Arabic joins; it does not stack
body: Say a phrase in your own language and notice that you do not pause between the words in it. Nobody does, in any language.
The pause you are producing in Arabic is an artefact of learning to read. It has to be actively removed; it will not fade on its own.
Reading joined is called waṣl, and it is the DEFAULT state of recitation. Stopping is the marked case — the thing you do deliberately.
Until now you have been doing the marked case at every single word.

Nothing new is introduced today. 2-10, 2-11, 2-12, 2-13 and 2-14 are one skill at five lengths — word, phrase, sentence, fluent sentence, page. What changes each time is only how much has to stay correct at once.

slides.heading: What actually happens at the seam — three things, and only three
body: Vowel, then consonant: just run on. Nothing special happens at all.
Vowel, then a waṣl hamzah: the hamzah vanishes. هُوَ ٱللَّهُ is huwa-llāhu.
Sukūn, then a waṣl hamzah: the hamzah vanishes AND the previous word takes a helping vowel. عَلَيْكُمُ ٱدْخُلُوا۟ is ʿalaykumu-dkhulū.
The muṣḥaf prints the helping vowel. You do not compute it; you read it. That removes the fear that joining requires grammar — it does not.

audio.cue: 113:2 — min sharri mā khalaq. Vowel into consonant, three times. Nothing to manage at any seam.
112:1 — huwa-llāhu. The alif is a step, not a sound. Step over it.
16:32 — ʿalaykumu-dkhulū. The mīm was sākin, so it borrowed a ḍammah, and the hamzah is gone.

slides.heading: The finger-slide
body: The most effective physical technique in this lesson.
Put a finger under the line and move it continuously at a steady speed while you read. Never stop it. Never lift it. All the way to the end of the phrase.
The finger cannot pause, so the voice cannot either.
And when the voice falls behind the finger, that gap is exactly where your reading is unstable — now both of us can SEE it, not just hear it.
If the voice cannot keep up, we slow the finger. We do not stop it.

slides.heading: Two words — one sound
slides.instructions: Finger under the line, moving steadily. The requirement at every rung is the same and it is binary: one sound, or not one sound. Accuracy of the individual words is assumed by now — if a word breaks, that is a 2-10 problem and it gets logged as one.

audio.cue: 113:2 — min sharri. Hold the doubled rāʾ and run straight on.
112:1 — qul huwa. A sukūn straight into a consonant. No vowel appears between them.
106:1 — li-īlāfi quraysh. A long madd and a līn, in two words.
104:6 — nāru-llāh. The waṣl hamzah of ٱللَّهِ vanishes after the ḍammah.

slides.heading: Three words
slides.instructions: Same requirement, one word longer. Breathe BEFORE the phrase, then read the whole thing.

audio.cue: 112:1 — huwa-llāhu aḥad. Your first dropped waṣl hamzah inside a phrase.
113:2 — min sharri mā khalaq. The easiest phrase in the hifz set; use it first when anything goes wrong.
113:1 — bi-rabbi-l-falaq. A doubled bāʾ held, then a joined waṣl hamzah.

slides.heading: Four to five words
slides.instructions: The top rung. This is where madds and shaddas start to shorten — not from ignorance, but because attention is divided. If the length collapses, halve the speed of the WHOLE phrase, not just the madd.

audio.cue: 1:2 — al-ḥamdu lillāhi rabbi-l-ʿālamīn. You START on a waṣl hamzah here, then join twice.
110:1 — idhā jāʾa naṣru-llāhi wal-fatḥ. Four words with a four-count madd in the middle that must survive the join.
108:2 — faṣalli li-rabbika wanḥar. A shadda at a word boundary running straight into a lām, then a joined waṣl hamzah.

slides.heading: Breath — take it before the phrase, not during it
body: Breathe. Read the whole phrase. Breathe.
If you cannot reach the end, the phrase is too long for your current breath — and that is INFORMATION, not failure.
Write down every phrase you could not finish. That list is the raw material for 2-12; the stopping plan you build next lesson is made out of it.
Today the rule is simple and absolute: finish the phrase, or start it again. Do not stop mid-phrase to breathe.
The nuance arrives in 2-12. Until then, running out of air is a measurement, and stopping mid-word is a habit worth not acquiring.

slides.heading: Glue the seam
slides.instructions: I say the last syllable of word one and the first syllable of word two, glued together — huwal-lā. You say it back. Then read the whole phrase. Do this for every seam in the graded set.

audio.cue: huwal-lā … huwa-llāhu. The seam is one syllable, not two words.
nārul-lā … nāru-llāh.
rabbil-fa … bi-rabbi-l-falaq.
kumud-khu … ʿalaykumu-dkhulū.

slides.heading: The graded eight — work them in this order
slides.instructions: The grading matters more than the content. Number 7, the basmalah, is the assessment item: if you can read it as one unbroken sound with all three hamzahs gone, you have this lesson.

audio.cue: 1 — four short words, no joins to manage.
2 — a long madd and a līn, two words.
3 — the first dropped waṣl hamzah in a phrase.
4 — shadda into a lām, then a joined waṣl hamzah.
5 — start ON a waṣl hamzah, then two joins.
6 — four words, a long madd in the middle.
7 — three waṣl hamzahs, all silent. The assessment item.
8 — the helping ḍammah, in the wild.

slides.heading: The trap — are you reading, or reciting?
slides.instructions: Read a phrase you know by heart. Then I cover one word with my finger and you tell me what is under it. If you cannot, you were reciting, not reading. Then read it uncovered, slowly, actually looking.

audio.cue: Cover ٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ. What is under my finger?
Cover ٱللَّهُ. What is under my finger?

slides.heading: Non-Qurʾānic phrases — nothing here is memorised
slides.instructions: These are the honest measurement. The Qurʾānic phrases are half-remembered and will flatter you. Finger under the line, one breath each.

audio.cue: Two waṣl hamzahs to drop in flight: dhahaba-l-waladu ila-l-madrasah.
A līn yāʾ, a dropped hamzah, and two tanwīns: fi-l-bayti kitābun jadīd.
A shadda held across a five-syllable word, then a join: al-mudarrisatu fi-l-jāmiʿah.
No waṣl hamzahs at all — pure vowel-into-consonant joining: hādhā ṣadīqī muḥammad.

slides.heading: Three seams, and what each one does

audio.cue: Vowel + consonant — run on. Nothing happens.
Vowel + waṣl hamzah — the hamzah vanishes.
Sukūn + waṣl hamzah — the hamzah vanishes and the previous word takes a printed helping vowel.
And the target: all three hamzahs gone, one unbroken sound, one breath.

slides.heading: Homework
tasks: The eight graded phrases, one breath each, five times a day, finger sliding.
Sūrat al-Falaq (113), read phrase by phrase, not word by word. Pencil a small arc over each group of words you intend to say in one breath, BEFORE you begin.
Write down every phrase you could not finish in one breath. Bring the list — 2-12 is built out of it.
The four non-Qurʾānic phrases, daily. These are the honest measurement; the Qurʾānic ones are half-remembered and will flatter you.

drills.title: The graded eight
drills.instructions: In order, one breath each, finger under the line and moving. Number 7 is the assessment item.

audio.cue: 1 — four short words, no joins.
2 — a long madd and a līn.
3 — first dropped waṣl hamzah in a phrase.
4 — shadda into a lām, then a joined waṣl hamzah.
5 — start on a waṣl hamzah, then two joins.
6 — four words, long madd in the middle.
7 — three silent waṣl hamzahs. The assessment item.
8 — the helping ḍammah in the wild.

drills.title: Glue the seam
drills.instructions: I say the glued seam, you say it back, then you read the whole phrase.

audio.cue: huwal-lā → huwa-llāhu.
nārul-lā → nāru-llāh.
rabbil-fa → bi-rabbi-l-falaq.
kumud-khu → ʿalaykumu-dkhulū.

drills.title: Non-Qurʾānic phrases
drills.instructions: Daily. Nothing here is memorised, so this is the honest measurement of whether joining is real.

audio.cue: dhahaba-l-waladu ila-l-madrasah.
fi-l-bayti kitābun jadīd.
al-mudarrisatu fi-l-jāmiʿah.
hādhā ṣadīqī muḥammad.

drills.title: One breath
drills.instructions: Breathe. Read the whole phrase. Breathe. If you run out before the end, tell me WHERE you ran out and write the phrase down — do not push through on empty lungs.

audio.cue: Five words. Where did the air go?
Five words with a four-count madd inside them.
Four words, and the one you know best — so any breath failure here is purely mechanical.

dailyChecklist: The eight graded phrases, one breath each, five times, finger sliding
Sūrat al-Falaq read phrase by phrase, with breath arcs pencilled in BEFORE reading
The four non-Qurʾānic phrases — the honest measurement
The running list of phrases that did not fit in one breath, added to daily
The basmalah as one unbroken sound, all three hamzahs gone

script: Open with the basmalah read carefully, word by word, in the 2-10 manner. She will hear the damage herself without any prompting from you — four words, three glottal stops, and a phrase that no longer sounds like the phrase.

Then say the sentence that justifies the hour: careful word-reading and correct phrase-reading are two different skills, and the first one done too well breaks the second. She has just spent a lesson being rewarded for the thing you are now asking her to stop.
Use her own language as the analogy for joining. Nobody pauses between words in any language; the pause is an artefact of learning to read, and it has to be removed deliberately.

Name waṣl as the DEFAULT and stopping as the marked case. She has, until now, been doing the marked case at every single word — that framing makes the correction feel like removing something rather than adding something.
The three seams are the entire technical content. Show each one on a real phrase and resist adding a fourth; there is not one.
Tell her outright that the muṣḥaf prints the helping vowel. The fear that joining requires grammar is what makes learners slow down at seams, and one sentence removes it.

The finger-slide is the highest-value technique in the lesson. The finger cannot pause, so the voice cannot either — and where the voice falls behind, both of you can now SEE the instability rather than only hear it. When she cannot keep up, slow the finger; never stop it.
Build the ladder inside the lesson — two words, then three, then four to five — exactly as 2-10 built it inside the word. At every rung the requirement is binary: one sound, or not one sound.
Assume word-level accuracy by now. If a word breaks, log it as a 2-10 problem and carry on; do not let phrase practice turn back into word practice.

Introduce breath lightly and make one rule absolute: finish the phrase or start it again, no stopping mid-phrase to breathe. The nuance is 2-12's job and giving it early costs that lesson its structure.
Note every phrase she cannot finish in one breath and make sure she writes them down too. That list IS next lesson's raw material — 2-12 is built out of it, not out of a generic sentence set.
Finish on the basmalah. If it comes out as one unbroken sound with all three hamzahs gone, she has 2-11.

listenFor.item: One unbroken stream of sound from the first letter of the phrase to the last, with the word boundaries audible only as rhythm — never as silence.
listenFor.commonMistake: A small silence at every word boundary — bismi · Allāhi · ar-raḥmāni.
listenFor.whyItHappens: She has spent nine lessons being rewarded for reading each word correctly, and the pause is where she checks her work. It is a CONFIDENCE behaviour, not an ignorance behaviour, which is why explaining the rule again does not remove it.
listenFor.correctionCue: Don't check. Trust the word you just read and keep going. If it was wrong I will tell you at the end.

listenFor.item: Nothing at all where a waṣl hamzah is written mid-phrase — the previous word running straight into the next letter.
listenFor.commonMistake: An audible glottal stop before every ٱ — huwa ʾal-lāhu.
listenFor.whyItHappens: The alif is visible on the page, and everything she has learned so far says READ WHAT IS WRITTEN. Silence is the one instruction the page gives by omission.
listenFor.correctionCue: The alif is a step, not a sound. Step over it — huwallāhu, one word.

listenFor.item: Madd counts and shadda holds surviving to the end of a five-word phrase, not just a two-word one.
listenFor.commonMistake: Madds and shaddas shorten as the phrase gets longer — correct in a two-word phrase, gone by five words.
listenFor.whyItHappens: Length is the first casualty of divided attention, exactly as in 2-10, and phrase-level joining is a heavier load than word-level accuracy.
listenFor.correctionCue: Halve the speed of the whole phrase. Everything in it gets longer, not just the madd.

listenFor.item: A breath taken before the phrase, sized for the whole distance.
listenFor.commonMistake: She reaches the end of her breath and either stops mid-word or forces a strained, thin last two words.
listenFor.whyItHappens: No breath plan — she began reading before deciding where she was going to end.
listenFor.correctionCue: Look at where the phrase ends before you breathe in. Breathe for the distance, not for the first word.

listenFor.item: One helping vowel at a sukūn seam, read off the page rather than invented.
listenFor.commonMistake: Either a second vowel added on the hamzah — ʿalaykumu idkhulū — or the printed helping vowel skipped entirely and two sākin letters collided.
listenFor.whyItHappens: The seam is the one place where the page's instruction is split across two words, and she is still reading one word at a time.
listenFor.correctionCue: The vowel is already printed, on the mīm. Read it, then keep going — there is nothing left to start.

teacherNotes.homework: Daily: the eight graded phrases one breath each, five times, with the finger sliding; Sūrat al-Falaq read phrase by phrase with the breath arcs pencilled in BEFORE she begins; the four non-Qurʾānic phrases, which are the only honest measurement since the Qurʾānic ones are half-remembered. Running, all week: a written list of every phrase she could not finish in one breath — she brings it to the next lesson, because 2-12's stopping plan is built directly out of it. The assessment item is the basmalah read as one unbroken sound with all three waṣl hamzahs silent.
